A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MEMENTO and retain the same core benchmark, agents, and experiments despite the revised title and expanded scope. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated agent results in Table 1, memory-format and ambiguous-instruction experiments in Tables 2–3, and additional memory-quality and knowledge-type analyses in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds user-profile memory experiments, a human baseline, annotator-agreement analysis, and memory robustness, retrieval, and generalization results.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's environmental scene graph and episodic memory, v2 introduces a separate hierarchical user-profile knowledge graph. It extracts and updates personalized knowledge, represents temporal relationships, and retrieves and reformulates subgraphs alongside episodic memory (Section 6.2; Appendix D.1). This adds a substantial memory-processing component.

E1.justification: The original 12-scene, 438-episode benchmark and ambiguous-instruction tasks remain. v2 substantially extends tested scenarios to three-memory coordination, transferring user patterns to changed target locations, corrupted or incomplete memories, and retrieval without guaranteed relevant memories (Appendix E), while retaining the household simulation domain.

E2.justification: The six-model headline comparison and three memory-format alternatives are retained. v2 adds an evaluated human reference (Appendix E.1) and compares LLM pointwise reranking and query expansion against embedding-only retrieval for GPT-4o and Qwen-2.5-72b (Table 11), substantially expanding comparison approaches.

E3.justification: The main metrics, oracle skills, and top-5 retrieval with guaranteed relevant memories remain. New experiments introduce distinct protocols: four human participants on 20 tasks, reranking ten candidates into top-3/top-5 results, 30% unrelated-step injection, 20% step removal, and separate graph-memory retrieval without guaranteed gold entries (Appendices D.3 and E).

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled tests of shuffled, injected, and removed memory steps; retrieval quality versus task success; three-memory coordination; and transfer to new locations. It also expands execution-trace case studies. These substantially extend the retained top-k, memory-quality, summarization, and ambiguous-instruction analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds inter-rater reliability estimation using Krippendorff's alpha, reporting four category values from 0.57 to 0.87 and an average of 0.69 (Appendix C.3.3). The five-attempt filtering procedure and existing 95% confidence intervals remain unchanged; no new seed counts or uncertainty estimates accompany agent-performance comparisons.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their scores, and v1's ambiguous-instruction results reappear in v2 Table 13. Substantial new results include user-profile memory gains in Figure 8 and robustness, retrieval, human, and transfer outcomes. Table 12 adds GPT-4o's 22.0% success rate on three-memory tasks; its retained two-memory result remains 63.9%, under different task requirements.

T1.justification: The POMDP, memory-dependent goal grounding, and paired/joint episode formulations are retained in condensed form. Making memory explicit in v2's policy notation restates conditioning already used in v1. The new graph schemas and pseudocode specify procedures without adding substantive mathematical assumptions, theoretical results, or proofs.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on introducing MEMENTO and diagnosing memory-utilization failures. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion additionally make a hierarchical user-profile memory architecture and its benefits on single- and joint-memory tasks central contributions, extending the paper from evaluation and diagnosis to a proposed solution.

C2.justification: v2 develops the rationale for separating personalized knowledge from episodic memory's in-context learning benefits. New interpretations concern retrieval improvements failing to ensure task success, navigation cues, and instruction cues supporting generalization. Appendix A also adds the absence of conversational clarification as a substantive limitation and expands privacy considerations.

D1.justification: v2 adds graph algorithms, node/edge schemas, construction and retrieval prompts, experimental configurations, explicit filtering criteria, complete trajectory/evaluation examples, and a code-access statement. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. Hardware and inference settings remain unchanged, while v1's separate asset-license and source-link appendix is omitted.

R1.justification: The main related-work coverage and earlier extended discussion are largely retained. v2 adds targeted connections to ConceptNet/COMET, context engineering, long-context modeling, retrieval methods, and annotation reliability. It also clarifies the distinction between explicitly provided user knowledge and preferences inferred from demonstrations.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion around three research questions. It combines and reorganizes the task/framework exposition, separates evaluation from bottleneck analysis, restructures the discussion around memory design, and reorganizes the appendices, including moving the ambiguous-instruction experiment out of the main text.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the framework overview and case taxonomy, adds overall bars and delta annotations to retained performance displays, and introduces user-profile memory plots and diagrams, schema tables, new experimental tables, and detailed trajectory tables. Extensive relocation and a changed document template further alter the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence beyond v1's guaranteed-retrieval evaluation through realistic retrieval and corruption tests, human solvability checks, and annotator-agreement analysis. It also documents and evaluates a concrete memory-design remedy. Small auxiliary studies, limited performance uncertainty reporting, and the contradiction between the no-human-subjects ethics statement and Appendix E.1 temper these gains, but the improved validation and explanatory reach provide a substantial net improvement.
